scope: Peterson and Davie, section 1.5.1, Bandwidth and Latency, at the source version identified in this package's provenance. Assess only the supplied passages and explicit problem assumptions.
terminology_policy: The opening passage uses bandwidth and throughput loosely as related terms. The later passage P03 distinguishes available link data rate from measured performance. Accept a student's loose terminology when their meaning is clear; probe the distinction before treating wording alone as an error. Do not teach that bandwidth in bits/s is signal propagation speed in m/s.

global_misconceptions.definition: The response is ambiguous, insufficient, inconsistent with more than one explanation, or does not fit a supported category.
global_misconceptions.handling: Store the actual response and uncertainty. Ask a neutral clarification when useful. This is an uncertainty label, not a diagnosed misconception.

misconception_policy: A wrong answer, omitted explanation, or arithmetic error alone is not evidence of a particular mental model. A response that explicitly states the relevant mistaken causal rule can motivate a tentative hypothesis, which must be tested with a targeted follow-up. Preserve evidence against the hypothesis; revise or dismiss it when contradicted. Never label a student with a proven misconception.

concepts.title: Bandwidth and measured throughput
objectives: Describe link bandwidth or data rate in bits per second and measured throughput as actual observed performance.
Calculate an observed data-transfer rate from a stated bit count and elapsed time.
Explain why a link's available data rate need not equal measured throughput.
Recognize that small exchanges and large transfers can emphasize different performance limits.
boundaries: Frequency-domain bandwidth in hertz is contextual reading, not an assessed objective.
Do not require explanations involving unassigned transport protocols, congestion-control algorithms, or detailed overhead accounting.
Application examples compare the stated conditions only; neither latency nor bandwidth always dominates.

common_misconceptions.definition: Treats a link's available data rate as a guarantee that an application achieves that measured rate.
common_misconceptions.evidence_that_may_support: Explicitly insists the observed rate must equal the stated link capacity despite supplied measurements.
common_misconceptions.diagnostic_caution: Using the words bandwidth and throughput interchangeably does not by itself support this hypothesis.

common_misconceptions.definition: Treats data rate and elapsed delay as the same quantity, or claims that raising data rate necessarily reduces every delay component.
common_misconceptions.evidence_that_may_support: An explanation equates bits per second with response time or assumes higher bandwidth necessarily changes propagation time.
common_misconceptions.diagnostic_caution: Bandwidth can reduce transmission time; a statement about a specific large transfer may be correct. Clarify the claim's scope.

concepts.title: Latency and round-trip time
objectives: Distinguish a stated one-way latency from a round-trip time.
State delay in units of time rather than bits per second.
Compute a round-trip duration from explicitly supplied forward and reverse delays under a negligible-response-processing assumption.
Recognize when one-way information is insufficient to determine a round trip.
boundaries: RTT is not universally twice a measured one-way delay; any equality of the two directions must be supplied as an assumption.
Do not require clock synchronization, routing, or protocol knowledge.
Latency is contextual: the source sometimes uses it generically, so identify the measurement's endpoints before scoring.

common_misconceptions.definition: Treats a stated one-way duration as already including the return journey.
common_misconceptions.evidence_that_may_support: Explains that a round-trip duration ends when the first message reaches the destination.
common_misconceptions.diagnostic_caution: The word latency alone is ambiguous in the source; use a prompt that explicitly says one-way.

common_misconceptions.definition: Assumes the reverse journey must have the same delay as the forward journey without a supporting assumption.
common_misconceptions.evidence_that_may_support: States that the return delay is necessarily identical, including when different directional delays are supplied.
common_misconceptions.diagnostic_caution: Twice the one-way delay is correct when equal directional delays are explicitly assumed.

concepts.title: Transmission delay
objectives: Explain transmission delay as the time needed to place a packet's bits onto the link at its given rate.
Use transmission delay = packet size in bits / link rate in bits per second.
Predict the effect of changing packet size or link rate while holding other relevant quantities fixed.
Explain why changing cable length alone changes propagation delay but not transmission delay.
boundaries: Use the stated effective transmission rate; do not substitute measured application throughput without an explicit instruction.
Use a single link with stated assumptions; do not infer extra hops when cable length changes.
Do not assess the source's simplifying one-bit remark in P08.

common_misconceptions.definition: Claims transmission delay increases with cable length when packet size and link transmission rate remain fixed.
common_misconceptions.evidence_that_may_support: Explicitly uses the greater travel distance as the reason transmission delay increases.
common_misconceptions.diagnostic_caution: The student may be using transmit colloquially for total delivery; first clarify which delay they mean.

common_misconceptions.definition: Treats putting packet bits onto a link and signal travel along that link as the same delay component.
common_misconceptions.evidence_that_may_support: Uses distance divided by signal speed as the transmission-delay calculation, or explicitly equates the two processes.
common_misconceptions.diagnostic_caution: Equal numerical values in one example do not mean the student thinks the concepts are identical.

concepts.title: Propagation delay
objectives: Explain propagation delay as signal travel time along a link.
Use propagation delay = cable length / effective signal speed in that medium.
Predict effects of changing distance or propagation speed while stating what remains fixed.
Distinguish propagation delay from effects of packet size and link data rate on transmission delay.
boundaries: Use the supplied signal speed; students need not memorize the medium-specific values.
Propagation delay is not the time until an entire packet finishes arriving; transmission contributes to whole-packet delivery.
No claims about the engineering feasibility of changing one parameter independently are assessed.

common_misconceptions.definition: Claims a larger packet takes longer for a given signal to traverse the same link at the same propagation speed.
common_misconceptions.evidence_that_may_support: Attributes increased propagation delay to the number of bits, rather than distinguishing the longer transmission time.
common_misconceptions.diagnostic_caution: A larger packet can finish arriving later because transmission takes longer; that statement alone is correct.

common_misconceptions.definition: Claims increasing the data rate necessarily increases the signal's travel speed along a link whose medium and propagation speed are fixed.
common_misconceptions.evidence_that_may_support: Uses link rate in bits/s as the denominator for propagation delay or says the signal moves faster because more bits are sent per second.
common_misconceptions.diagnostic_caution: Real upgrades may change several physical properties. Diagnose only within a controlled prompt that fixes propagation speed.

concepts.title: Queuing delay and total latency
objectives: Identify time a packet waits inside a switch before forwarding as queuing delay.
Distinguish waiting from transmission and propagation.
Add supplied propagation, transmission, and queue components in the source's simplified latency model.
Find an unknown queue component from a supplied total and the other two components.
boundaries: Every numerical queue duration is supplied directly or follows by subtraction from supplied component totals.
Do not assess queue distributions, traffic intensity, arrival rates, utilization, packet loss, or scheduling theory.
The simplified three-component model is assumed in the questions; do not imply it is exhaustive for every real network.

common_misconceptions.definition: Treats waiting for forwarding to begin as the same process as placing packet bits onto the outbound link.
common_misconceptions.evidence_that_may_support: Labels an explicitly stated waiting interval as transmission or omits it because transmission time has already been counted.
common_misconceptions.diagnostic_caution: A simple summation mistake does not establish conceptual confusion. Ask the student to label the intervals.

common_misconceptions.definition: Claims every packet must experience a positive queue wait even when immediate forwarding is specified.
common_misconceptions.evidence_that_may_support: Insists that a positive wait must be added to an example that explicitly gives zero waiting time.
common_misconceptions.diagnostic_caution: The source says queue delays may occur; do not ask students to predict queue time from unstated traffic conditions.
